title: The summit: the Guru that stays
hookLine: ten lights now shine in the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat; the Guru goes with you from here
tomorrow: the summit's done. so where does the path go from here?

cards: The kitchen light again, before dawn. This time Simran is the one at the table, reading the day's hukam aloud from her phone, line by slow line, and Bebe is the one half listening, her bad knee up on a chair.
When Simran finishes, Bebe asks the question she's been saving all summer: and out there, who's your Guru? After ten Gurus, who is the Guru now? Simran doesn't need the phone for this one.

teach.b: Today's question is the one the whole climb has led to: where is the Guru now?

Tradition says that before Guru Gobind Singh died, he placed the Guruship in the scripture, and the line sung after the Ardas says it, in paraphrase: all Sikhs are ordered to accept the Granth as the Guru.
Guru Ram Das had already said it, on Ang 982.
In paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word. And the bards on Ang 966: the light is the same; only the body changed.
Ten bodies, one light, and now the light lives in the Word, and in the sangat gathered around it. A neighbor tradition opens a Gospel with the Word too.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.
teach.b: In the King James words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." What's shared: the Word as the place where God meets people.
The honest difference: John goes on to say the Word was made flesh, one person, Jesus. For Sikhs, the light passed through ten Gurus and now rests in the Word itself, and in the gathered community.

teach.h: A BOOK, AND A ROOM OF PEOPLE.
teach.b: One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh Guru today is a book you can open and a room of people you can sit with. Simran answers Bebe: the same one as yours.
Bebe says waheguru, and drinks her tea.

how: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru: it is opened each morning, read and sung from, covered when closed, and the sangat gathers before it; Sikhs often say 'Waheguru' in remembrance, and the line 'Guru maaniyo Granth' is sung after the Ardas.

o: the day the Sikh path ends and the Gurus are gone
the top of the climb: the Guru stays, in the Word and sangat
a mountain pilgrimage Sikhs make once in their lives

games.q: the Guru that stays — tap the pairs.
p: accept the Granth as the Guru
the Word is the Guru, the Guru the Word
the same light; only the body changed
in the beginning was the Word

s: since the tenth Guru died, Sikhs have had no Guru
the Guruship rests in the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat.
the Gospel of John and Guru Ram Das both speak of the Word
shared: the Word where God meets people. different: John says the Word was made flesh.
Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as a history book
they honor it as the living Guru: the Word is the Guru.

games.q: your new roommate sees you reading from your phone at dawn and asks who your guru is, since your Gurus lived long ago. what do you say?
o: the last human Guru; there hasn't been a Guru since he died.
any teacher you choose; Sikhs pick their own personal guru.
the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat: the same light, in the Word.
games.why: the light passed through ten Gurus and rests in the Word, the Granth, and in the gathered sangat. the Guru goes with you.

practice: If a Guru Granth Sahib or a gutka is near, open it and read one line slowly. If not, bow your head where you are, hands together or open in your lap.
Let the word waheguru, or simply a breath of thanks, rest there for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: The summit: ten Gurus, one light, now in the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat. The Guru goes with you from here.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Waheguru, the Sikh name for the One, said in wonder.

carryVoice: The last line of the climb: waheguru, wonder at the One, from the first Guru's sky to a kitchen table. The summit, reached.
